title: More Than the Builder

storyBibleReview.storySpine: Kit wants to speak in the class puppet show as well as build its stage, but Zoe assumes he only wants the building job.
storyBibleReview.failedAttempt: He rehearses behind the stage without explaining what he wants, and Zoe mistakes his voice practice for a sound effect.

title: One Story, Two Endings

storyBibleReview.storySpine: Zoe and Kit want to finish a shared picture story, but each removes the other’s ending because they want different things from it.
storyBibleReview.failedAttempt: Kit replaces Zoe’s quiet reunion with a comic surprise, then Zoe hides his new page; the book no longer has a shared ending.

title: A Garden for the Rain

storyBibleReview.topicQuestion: How can a community reduce water rushing from roofs and paths toward a stream?
storyBibleReview.progression: Trace rainfall across hard surfaces, identify runoff and carried dirt, then follow a deliberately built planted hollow and its overflow route.
storyBibleReview.synthesis: A rain garden slows and holds some runoff so it can soak into suitable ground; it complements drainage rather than making floods impossible.

scienceSources.title: EPA: Types of Green Infrastructure
scienceSources.evidence: Rain gardens are shallow planted depressions collecting runoff and filtering through soil; bioretention may infiltrate or use an underdrain.

scienceSources.title: Massachusetts: Stormwater Solutions for Homeowners—Rain Gardens
scienceSources.evidence: Rain gardens collect roof and paved-area runoff, reduce offsite runoff and require appropriate siting, soil and design.

scienceSources.title: EPA: What You Can Do to Soak Up the Rain
scienceSources.evidence: Hard surfaces produce runoff that can transport pollutants; planted practices reduce but do not eliminate runoff.

setting: One neighborhood community building beside a paved path and stream. A mature shallow rain garden sits safely away from foundations and the walking route. On page 7 only, two unnamed adult planners stand beside the garden: a woman with deep brown skin, short black curls, navy work shirt and gray trousers; a man with fair skin, short brown hair, green work shirt and tan trousers. This page explains planning, not a new rain event.

title: The Door in the Chalk

storyBibleReview.storySpine: Zoe must carry a large paper moon into the next room for a puppet show, but even a magic chalk doorway fails if its outline is too narrow or broken.
storyBibleReview.failedAttempt: Her first complete doorway is tall but too narrow for the moon; later a rubbed gap closes the wider opening while Kit is in the next room.
storyBibleReview.resolution: Zoe uses the moon’s width to draw a wider continuous outline, then repairs a visible gap to reopen the same passage for Kit.
storyBibleReview.magicRule: An unbroken silver chalk outline makes an opening only into the space immediately beyond the wall. Any gap closes it; rejoining the gap reopens it. The opening has exactly the drawn width and height, and cannot shrink or soften solid objects. Erasing the complete outline removes that opening.

title: The River Moves the Bank

storyBibleReview.topicQuestion: How can a river change the land along its bends?
storyBibleReview.progression: Compare two sides of a bend, follow erosion and carried sediment, then observe deposition and the changed channel over time.
storyBibleReview.synthesis: Water can remove ground in one place and leave sediment elsewhere, so a river’s edges change through connected processes.

scienceSources.title: NatureScot: How rivers and burns work
scienceSources.evidence: River flow controls sediment transport. Moderate flows carry smaller grains in suspension; stronger flows can roll and move larger material.

scienceSources.title: US Army Corps of Engineers: Sediment Changes the Depth and Shape
scienceSources.evidence: Sediment transport, erosion and deposition alter river depth and shape; riverbank erosion and sedimentation are observable connected processes.

scienceSources.title: National Park Service: Fluvial Features—Meandering Stream
scienceSources.evidence: Faster flow toward the outside of a bend erodes the outer bank, while reduced current deposits sediment on the inside. These connected changes move a meander over time.

setting: One gently winding river in a grassy valley over months, with a steep outer bank and low inner sandbar. A solitary broad tree remains beyond the outer bank as a position reference.
coverBrief: Elevated view of one river bend contrasts a steep worn outer bank with a low pale sandbar on the inside, preserving a clear downstream channel.

pages.text: This river bend has two very different edges. One bank is steep. Across the water, a low strip of sand slopes gently.
pages.imageBrief: Elevated view of river bend shows steep outer bank with exposed soil opposite low sandy inner bank. Exact continuity: Single bend; no reversing upstream/downstream; tree beyond steep bank.
pages.imageAlt: Elevated view of river bend shows steep outer bank with exposed soil opposite low sandy inner bank.
pages.pageDescription: Elevated view of river bend shows steep outer bank with exposed soil opposite low sandy inner bank.
pages.state: Single bend; no reversing upstream/downstream; tree beyond steep bank.

pages.text: Moving water can loosen soil and carry it away. That wearing away is called erosion. Watch the outside of the bend.
pages.imageBrief: Close view shows water at base of outer bank carrying a little loosened brown soil downstream. Exact continuity: No explosive landslide; small erosion at water contact; tree remains inland.
pages.imageAlt: Close view shows water at base of outer bank carrying a little loosened brown soil downstream.
pages.pageDescription: Close view shows water at base of outer bank carrying a little loosened brown soil downstream.
pages.state: No explosive landslide; small erosion at water contact; tree remains inland.

pages.text: Here, faster water presses against the bank. Bits of soil fall into the flow, leaving the edge farther back.
pages.imageBrief: Outer bank has a small fresh notch at waterline and loose soil entering the river. Exact continuity: Same bank retreating gradually; no child near unstable edge.
pages.imageAlt: Outer bank has a small fresh notch at waterline and loose soil entering the river.
pages.pageDescription: Outer bank has a small fresh notch at waterline and loose soil entering the river.
pages.state: Same bank retreating gradually; no child near unstable edge.

pages.text: The river carries this loose material, called sediment. Fine grains travel in the water; heavier pieces may roll below.
pages.imageBrief: Underwater cutaway shows fine suspended sediment and a few small pebbles rolling along the bed. Exact continuity: Cutaway explanatory; grains enlarged enough to see without implying pebble-sized silt.
pages.imageAlt: Underwater cutaway shows fine suspended sediment and a few small pebbles rolling along the bed.
pages.pageDescription: Underwater cutaway shows fine suspended sediment and a few small pebbles rolling along the bed.
pages.state: Cutaway explanatory; grains enlarged enough to see without implying pebble-sized silt.

pages.text: Where the current slows, it cannot keep carrying the same load. Some sediment settles onto the riverbed.
pages.imageBrief: Widening shallow section inside bend shows sand settling onto a low bar beneath slow-moving water. Exact continuity: No animated hands or intention; deposition shown physically.
pages.imageAlt: Widening shallow section inside bend shows sand settling onto a low bar beneath slow-moving water.
pages.pageDescription: Widening shallow section inside bend shows sand settling onto a low bar beneath slow-moving water.
pages.state: No animated hands or intention; deposition shown physically.

pages.text: Leaving sediment behind is called deposition. On the inside of this bend, sand collects into a shallow bar.
pages.imageBrief: Pale sandbar occupies inside of bend with a damp edge and a few settled pebbles. Exact continuity: Same bar as opening; growth gradual, no instant dry island.
pages.imageAlt: Pale sandbar occupies inside of bend with a damp edge and a few settled pebbles.
pages.pageDescription: Pale sandbar occupies inside of bend with a damp edge and a few settled pebbles.
pages.state: Same bar as opening; growth gradual, no instant dry island.

pages.text: Over time, the outside edge wears back while the inside bar grows. The curve of the river slowly shifts.
pages.imageBrief: Wider view after elapsed months shows larger inner sandbar and farther-back outer bank, tree still fixed beyond it. Exact continuity: Same tree anchors comparison; no duplicate ghost river or unlabeled overlay.
pages.imageAlt: Wider view after elapsed months shows larger inner sandbar and farther-back outer bank, tree still fixed beyond it.
pages.pageDescription: Wider view after elapsed months shows larger inner sandbar and farther-back outer bank, tree still fixed beyond it.
pages.state: Same tree anchors comparison; no duplicate ghost river or unlabeled overlay.

pages.text: A heavy flow can move larger pieces than a gentle flow. After a storm, the bank and bar may change more quickly.
pages.imageBrief: Higher brownish river flow carries pebbles along bank; grass above water and fixed tree establish location. Exact continuity: Storm effect is possible, not every flood identical; no humans in floodwater.
pages.imageAlt: Higher brownish river flow carries pebbles along bank; grass above water and fixed tree establish location.
pages.pageDescription: Higher brownish river flow carries pebbles along bank; grass above water and fixed tree establish location.
pages.state: Storm effect is possible, not every flood identical; no humans in floodwater.

pages.text: When the water drops, fresh sand remains. The river has not simply taken land away; it has left material in new places.
pages.imageBrief: Lower river level reveals new damp sand on inside bar and a newly exposed outer-bank face. Exact continuity: Sediment retained after flood; no claim equal amounts everywhere.
pages.imageAlt: Lower river level reveals new damp sand on inside bar and a newly exposed outer-bank face.
pages.pageDescription: Lower river level reveals new damp sand on inside bar and a newly exposed outer-bank face.
pages.state: Sediment retained after flood; no claim equal amounts everywhere.

pages.text: Look again at the steep bank and sandy bar. One bend shows two connected changes: ground removed here and sediment left there.
pages.imageBrief: Final elevated view balances steep eroded outer edge and broad deposited inner bar in same frame. Exact continuity: Clear two-process synthesis; tree remains in original position; no printed labels.
pages.imageAlt: Final elevated view balances steep eroded outer edge and broad deposited inner bar in same frame.
pages.pageDescription: Final elevated view balances steep eroded outer edge and broad deposited inner bar in same frame.
pages.state: Clear two-process synthesis; tree remains in original position; no printed labels.

oral.prompt: How are the steep bank and sandy bar connected?
oral.listenFor: Water erodes and carries sediment, then deposits some where flow slows; removal and buildup reshape the same bend.

visual.prompt: Where has ground been worn away, and where has material built up?
visual.lookFor: Steep outer bank shows erosion; low inner bar shows deposition.

levelRationale: App E links two simultaneous processes, transport capacity, changing flow and elapsed time. The reader must connect removal and deposition across separate places while retaining the same river bend.

title: The Moon Has Not Shrunk

storyBibleReview.topicQuestion: Why does the Moon look like a thin curve on some evenings and a bright circle on others?
storyBibleReview.progression: Distinguish the whole Moon from its sunlit half, change the observer’s view as it orbits Earth, and connect that geometry to the repeating phases.
storyBibleReview.synthesis: The Moon stays round; phases are changing views of its sunlit half, not pieces disappearing or the ordinary effect of Earth’s shadow.

scienceSources.title: NASA Science: Moon Phases
scienceSources.evidence: The Moon remains a sphere with a sunlit half. Our view of that half changes as it orbits; the phase cycle takes about 29.5 days. Northern-view waxing crescents and first quarter are lit on the right.

scienceSources.title: NASA Science: Moon Facts
scienceSources.evidence: The Moon is Earth’s natural satellite; orbital geometry determines illumination seen from Earth, while eclipses require alignment.

scienceSources.title: NASA Science: Eclipses and the Moon
scienceSources.evidence: Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse; the tilted lunar orbit prevents eclipses every month. This differs from ordinary phases caused by changing viewpoint.

setting: Diagrammatic space views of Sun, Earth and Moon, then Earth-sky views across the lunar month. Distances and sizes explicitly simplified; no named characters.
props: Sun outside or at far left
Thin crescent and full-disk sky views
coverBrief: A large round Moon shows a bright crescent and a faint remaining disk against deep blue sky, making the whole spherical shape clear without a face.

pages.text: One evening, the Moon looks like a thin curved slice. Later, it looks round and bright. Has part of it disappeared?
pages.imageBrief: Single evening-sky view shows a thin bright lunar crescent with its full dark circular outline faintly visible. Exact continuity: One Moon only; no literal cutout or bitten edge.
pages.imageAlt: Single evening-sky view shows a thin bright lunar crescent with its full dark circular outline faintly visible.
pages.pageDescription: Single evening-sky view shows a thin bright lunar crescent with its full dark circular outline faintly visible.
pages.state: One Moon only; no literal cutout or bitten edge.

pages.text: The Moon is still a whole round world. Sunlight lights the half facing the Sun, while the other half is dark.
pages.imageBrief: Space view shows a spherical Moon with left hemisphere illuminated by light arriving from far left. Exact continuity: Half sphere lit; no Earth shadow involved; no stars showing through dark side.
pages.imageAlt: Space view shows a spherical Moon with left hemisphere illuminated by light arriving from far left.
pages.pageDescription: Space view shows a spherical Moon with left hemisphere illuminated by light arriving from far left.
pages.state: Half sphere lit; no Earth shadow involved; no stars showing through dark side.

pages.text: But we watch from Earth, not from the Sun. We do not always see the entire sunlit half.
pages.imageBrief: A simplified top-down space view places Earth near the lower center and one Moon above it, with sunlight arriving parallel from the far left. The Moon’s left half is sunlit and its right half dark; the Earth–Moon direction is about a right angle to the incoming sunlight. Exact continuity: Not to scale; one Moon; Earth and Moon illuminated from the same leftward source; no Earth shadow crossing the Moon.
pages.imageAlt: A simplified top-down space view places Earth near the lower center and one Moon above it, with sunlight arriving parallel from the far left. The Moon’s left half is sunlit and its right half dark; the Earth–Moon direction is about a right angle to the incoming sunlight.
pages.pageDescription: A simplified top-down space view places Earth near the lower center and one Moon above it, with sunlight arriving parallel from the far left. The Moon’s left half is sunlit and its right half dark; the Earth–Moon direction is about a right angle to the incoming sunlight.
pages.state: Not to scale; one Moon; Earth and Moon illuminated from the same leftward source; no Earth shadow crossing the Moon.

pages.text: As the Moon travels around Earth, our view changes. Different amounts of the bright half face toward us.
pages.imageBrief: In the same simplified top-down view, Earth stays fixed and one Moon now lies upper-left of Earth. Sunlight still arrives from far left, illuminating the Moon’s left hemisphere; its angle as seen from Earth differs from page 3. Exact continuity: New illustrative orbital position, not a labeled phase chronology; one Moon only; unchanged light direction; no arrows or duplicate ghosts.
pages.imageAlt: In the same simplified top-down view, Earth stays fixed and one Moon now lies upper-left of Earth. Sunlight still arrives from far left, illuminating the Moon’s left hemisphere; its angle as seen from Earth differs from page 3.
pages.pageDescription: In the same simplified top-down view, Earth stays fixed and one Moon now lies upper-left of Earth. Sunlight still arrives from far left, illuminating the Moon’s left hemisphere; its angle as seen from Earth differs from page 3.
pages.state: New illustrative orbital position, not a labeled phase chronology; one Moon only; unchanged light direction; no arrows or duplicate ghosts.

pages.text: Near new moon, the sunlit half mostly faces away from Earth. The Moon is usually hard to see in the bright sky.
pages.imageBrief: Diagram shows Moon between Sun direction and Earth but slightly above direct alignment, dark lunar side facing Earth. Exact continuity: No eclipse alignment; Sun not covered; Moon’s lit half faces away from Earth.
pages.imageAlt: Diagram shows Moon between Sun direction and Earth but slightly above direct alignment, dark lunar side facing Earth.
pages.pageDescription: Diagram shows Moon between Sun direction and Earth but slightly above direct alignment, dark lunar side facing Earth.
pages.state: No eclipse alignment; Sun not covered; Moon’s lit half faces away from Earth.

pages.text: A few days later, a bright crescent appears. We can see only a narrow part of the Moon’s sunlit half.
pages.imageBrief: An Earth-sky view of a young evening crescent above a quiet western horizon shows a narrow bright curve on the right, with the full dark disk subtly retained. Exact continuity: Chosen northern-hemisphere evening viewpoint; illuminated edge faces the unseen setting Sun; no universal right-side rule printed.
pages.imageAlt: An Earth-sky view of a young evening crescent above a quiet western horizon shows a narrow bright curve on the right, with the full dark disk subtly retained.
pages.pageDescription: An Earth-sky view of a young evening crescent above a quiet western horizon shows a narrow bright curve on the right, with the full dark disk subtly retained.
pages.state: Chosen northern-hemisphere evening viewpoint; illuminated edge faces the unseen setting Sun; no universal right-side rule printed.

pages.text: About a week after new moon, half the Moon’s face looks bright. The whole Moon has not changed shape.
pages.imageBrief: An Earth-sky view shows a first-quarter Moon with the right half of the visible disk bright and the left half dark, against an early evening sky. Exact continuity: Same chosen northern-hemisphere viewpoint; round disk remains whole; no physical half-sphere cut away.
pages.imageAlt: An Earth-sky view shows a first-quarter Moon with the right half of the visible disk bright and the left half dark, against an early evening sky.
pages.pageDescription: An Earth-sky view shows a first-quarter Moon with the right half of the visible disk bright and the left half dark, against an early evening sky.
pages.state: Same chosen northern-hemisphere viewpoint; round disk remains whole; no physical half-sphere cut away.

pages.text: Near full moon, Earth faces almost all of the sunlit half. The bright disk looks round again.
pages.imageBrief: Full round Moon appears above horizon with consistent craters; all visible face illuminated. Exact continuity: Do not place Earth’s shadow over Moon; no claim full Moon has no dark far hemisphere.
pages.imageAlt: Full round Moon appears above horizon with consistent craters; all visible face illuminated.
pages.pageDescription: Full round Moon appears above horizon with consistent craters; all visible face illuminated.
pages.state: Do not place Earth’s shadow over Moon; no claim full Moon has no dark far hemisphere.

pages.text: After that, the bright part we see gets smaller. The pattern repeats in about a month as the Moon keeps orbiting.
pages.imageBrief: A later-month predawn view above the eastern horizon shows a waning crescent bright on the left, with the same full circular outline and matching crater geography. Exact continuity: Later stage before sunrise, not an evening waning crescent; chosen northern-hemisphere viewpoint; no literal shrinking of diameter.
pages.imageAlt: A later-month predawn view above the eastern horizon shows a waning crescent bright on the left, with the same full circular outline and matching crater geography.
pages.pageDescription: A later-month predawn view above the eastern horizon shows a waning crescent bright on the left, with the same full circular outline and matching crater geography.
pages.state: Later stage before sunrise, not an evening waning crescent; chosen northern-hemisphere viewpoint; no literal shrinking of diameter.

pages.text: These changing views are called phases. Earth’s shadow makes a lunar eclipse, a different event. Ordinary phases come from our changing viewpoint.
pages.imageBrief: Space view shows Sun direction, Earth and Moon off exact alignment, with a clear sightline toward partly illuminated Moon. Exact continuity: No eclipse shown; whole sphere and sunlit half remain; final diagram reinforces viewpoint, not shadow covering.
pages.imageAlt: Space view shows Sun direction, Earth and Moon off exact alignment, with a clear sightline toward partly illuminated Moon.
pages.pageDescription: Space view shows Sun direction, Earth and Moon off exact alignment, with a clear sightline toward partly illuminated Moon.
pages.state: No eclipse shown; whole sphere and sunlit half remain; final diagram reinforces viewpoint, not shadow covering.

oral.prompt: What changes during the Moon’s ordinary phases, and what stays the same?
oral.listenFor: Our view of its sunlit half changes as it orbits; the Moon remains a whole sphere. Earth’s shadow is an eclipse.

visual.prompt: What tells you the Moon is still whole when only half looks bright?
visual.lookFor: The dark half completes the round disk; light and dark divide its visible face.

levelRationale: App E coordinates two viewpoints, a sunlit hemisphere and a month-long orbital sequence. The distinction between actual shape, visible illumination and eclipse requires supported conceptual inference.

title: A Flower’s Night Visitor

storyBibleReview.topicQuestion: How can a nectar-feeding bat help a cactus while getting its own meal?
storyBibleReview.progression: Follow a lesser long-nosed bat to a night-opening saguaro flower, observe nectar feeding and pollen transfer, then connect pollination to later fruit and seeds.
storyBibleReview.synthesis: Bat and cactus benefit through one connected visit: nectar feeds the bat and transferred pollen helps the cactus reproduce.

scienceSources.title: National Park Service: Lesser Long-nosed Bats
scienceSources.evidence: Nectar-feeding lesser long-nosed bats visit night-blooming saguaro flowers; long noses and tongues reach nectar, pollen coats their heads and transfers between flowers.

scienceSources.title: University of Arizona Cooperative Extension: Saguaro Cactus
scienceSources.evidence: Saguaros are pollinated by bats, birds and insects; fruits contain many seeds, which animals can disperse.

setting: Sonoran Desert at night during saguaro flowering, followed by a later fruiting view in daylight. One lesser long-nosed bat with natural brown fur and long muzzle.
props: Saguaro cactus with creamy white flowers near top
Later red saguaro fruit and dark seeds

pages.text: This lesser long-nosed bat drinks nectar, the sweet liquid inside flowers. Its long muzzle fits into the open bloom.

title: A Frog Changes Its Way of Life

storyBibleReview.topicQuestion: How does a pond tadpole become a frog able to live at the water’s edge?
storyBibleReview.progression: Follow a common frog through eggs, aquatic tadpole, changing legs/tail/breathing structures, froglet and adult returning to breed.
storyBibleReview.synthesis: Metamorphosis changes several connected body systems, and the adult’s return to water starts another generation rather than returning its own life to the beginning.

scienceSources.title: Natural History Museum: Frogspawn, tadpoles and froglets
scienceSources.evidence: Common frogs lay frogspawn in clumps; tadpoles and froglets can be observed as seasonal stages in ponds. The Australian Museum source supplies the detailed metamorphosis explanation.

scienceSources.title: Australian Museum: Frog life cycle
scienceSources.evidence: Typical frog metamorphosis includes internal changes; tail is absorbed rather than shed; adults use lungs and moist skin. Frog species have exceptions, so manuscript names common frog.

pages.text: Front legs appeared, too. Inside, its body was changing: lungs developed while its gills became less important.
pages.imageBrief: A later common-frog tadpole with four legs rises near the surface, its long tail still attached; the view shows only its natural external body. Exact continuity: Four legs plus tail is a metamorph stage; no abrupt no-overlap breathing claim; no speculative cutaway anatomy or external lung balloons.
pages.imageAlt: A later common-frog tadpole with four legs rises near the surface, its long tail still attached; the view shows only its natural external body.
pages.pageDescription: A later common-frog tadpole with four legs rises near the surface, its long tail still attached; the view shows only its natural external body.
pages.state: Four legs plus tail is a metamorph stage; no abrupt no-overlap breathing claim; no speculative cutaway anatomy or external lung balloons.

pages.text: The tail did not fall off. The body absorbed it, using its materials as the young frog continued to change.
pages.imageBrief: Froglet with four strong legs and a visibly shorter tail rests in shallow water. Exact continuity: Tail stub attached smoothly; no detached tail or injury.

pages.state: Tail stub attached smoothly; no detached tail or injury.

pages.text: Now the froglet could climb onto a damp bank. Its new legs, lungs, and changing body helped it use another place.
pages.imageBrief: Small froglet climbs a moist low bank from shallow pond water; short tail stub remains. Exact continuity: No dry desert habitat; froglet stays near moisture.
pages.imageAlt: Small froglet climbs a moist low bank from shallow pond water; short tail stub remains.
pages.pageDescription: Small froglet climbs a moist low bank from shallow pond water; short tail stub remains.
pages.state: No dry desert habitat; froglet stays near moisture.

pages.text: Adult common frogs breathe with lungs and moist skin. They can hunt small animals on land, but they still need damp places.
pages.imageBrief: Adult brown common frog crouches in damp grass beside pond, facing a tiny insect at natural distance. Exact continuity: No human mouth or clothes; skin moist, no scaly reptile surface.
pages.imageAlt: Adult brown common frog crouches in damp grass beside pond, facing a tiny insect at natural distance.
pages.pageDescription: Adult brown common frog crouches in damp grass beside pond, facing a tiny insect at natural distance.

pages.text: When breeding time comes, adults return to water. New eggs begin another generation, not the same frog’s life all over again.
pages.imageBrief: Two adult common frogs are near a fresh egg clump in pond shallows during a later breeding season. Exact continuity: Adults natural mating context without explicit anatomy; new eggs distinct generation.
pages.imageAlt: Two adult common frogs are near a fresh egg clump in pond shallows during a later breeding season.
pages.pageDescription: Two adult common frogs are near a fresh egg clump in pond shallows during a later breeding season.

pages.text: Egg, tadpole, froglet, adult: the changes fit different ways of living. A tiny swimmer becomes a frog at the water’s edge.
pages.imageBrief: Final adult common frog at original moist bank, with young tadpoles in the shallows below. Exact continuity: Adults and new-generation tadpoles coexist; not a lineup of identical individuals frozen at once.
pages.imageAlt: Final adult common frog at original moist bank, with young tadpoles in the shallows below.

oral.prompt: Why is changing from a tadpole to a frog more than just growing legs?
oral.listenFor: The tail is absorbed and breathing structures change as legs develop, helping the young frog move from swimming underwater to using damp banks.

visual.prompt: Find the froglet’s tail. What is still attached to its body?
visual.lookFor: A smaller attached tail stub remains; there is no separate discarded tail.

levelRationale: App E integrates multiple body changes, overlapping development and a return across generations. Temporal shifts and careful distinctions between growth, metamorphosis and reproduction require sustained explanation.

title: A Whale Is Not a Fish

storyBibleReview.topicQuestion: Why do scientists place whales with mammals even though whales live and swim among fish?
storyBibleReview.progression: Start with similar habitat and body shape, compare breathing and feeding young, then reject a single-clue shortcut and apply multiple biological traits.
storyBibleReview.synthesis: Classification uses related body features and ways of living; a shared habitat or one superficially similar trait does not make animals the same kind.

scienceSources.title: NOAA: Marine mammals
scienceSources.evidence: Marine mammals breathe air with lungs, maintain body heat, have hair during some life stage and nurse young with milk.

scienceSources.title: NOAA Ocean Service: Are dolphins fish?
scienceSources.evidence: Dolphins use lungs and a blowhole and nurse young with milk; whales, dolphins and porpoises are mammals.

scienceSources.title: NOAA Fisheries: Whales
scienceSources.evidence: Whales are cetacean marine mammals; baleen and toothed whales form distinct groups.

scienceSources.title: NOAA Fisheries: Sandbar Shark
scienceSources.evidence: Sandbar sharks are fish that give birth to live young in shallow nursery grounds.

scienceSources.title: Smithsonian Ocean: Whales and Dolphins
scienceSources.evidence: Baleen whales have two blowholes; toothed whales and dolphins have one.

scienceSources.title: NOAA: How marine mammals stay warm
scienceSources.evidence: Blubber insulates marine mammals in cold water.

scienceSources.title: National Park Service: Blue Whale
scienceSources.evidence: A female blue whale gives birth to a calf, which grows while nursing. The live-born calf supplies the comparison before the separate live-bearing shark example.

setting: Ocean habitat with one blue whale and calf and a small school of bony fish; occasional clear comparison views, no human characters.
props: Small silver bony fish with gill covers
coverBrief: A blue whale and its smaller calf swim below the ocean surface while a small school of silver fish passes beneath, making shared habitat and different bodies visible.

pages.text: A whale swims past a school of fish. Both have streamlined bodies for swimming. Why are they placed in different groups?
pages.imageBrief: Adult blue whale swims above small silver fish in a clear underwater scene. Exact continuity: Whale much larger; horizontal tail flukes and fish vertical tails correct.
pages.imageAlt: Adult blue whale swims above small silver fish in a clear underwater scene.
pages.pageDescription: Adult blue whale swims above small silver fish in a clear underwater scene.
pages.state: Whale much larger; horizontal tail flukes and fish vertical tails correct.

pages.text: Living in the same place does not make animals the same kind. Their bodies and life histories give us more clues.
pages.imageBrief: Wide ocean view retains whale and fish in separate depths, each using its own body shape to swim. Exact continuity: Same ocean habitat; different animal groups remain distinct. No literal family tree or labels.
pages.imageAlt: Wide ocean view retains whale and fish in separate depths, each using its own body shape to swim.
pages.pageDescription: Wide ocean view retains whale and fish in separate depths, each using its own body shape to swim.
pages.state: Same ocean habitat; different animal groups remain distinct. No literal family tree or labels.

pages.text: Watch the whale rise. It takes air into lungs through blowholes on top of its head, then dives while holding its breath.
pages.imageBrief: The blue whale’s head reaches the surface with both blowholes clear of the water as it takes in air. Exact continuity: Blue whale has paired blowholes; this moment is inhalation, so no outward spray or water fountain; fish remain underwater.
pages.imageAlt: The blue whale’s head reaches the surface with both blowholes clear of the water as it takes in air.
pages.pageDescription: The blue whale’s head reaches the surface with both blowholes clear of the water as it takes in air.
pages.state: Blue whale has paired blowholes; this moment is inhalation, so no outward spray or water fountain; fish remain underwater.

pages.text: The fish stay below. Their gills take oxygen from water passing over them. They do not need the whale’s surface-breathing routine.
pages.imageBrief: Close side view of silver bony fish shows normal gill covers behind eyes as water flows past. Exact continuity: No human lung graphic in fish; no universal claim every fish never breathes air.
pages.imageAlt: Close side view of silver bony fish shows normal gill covers behind eyes as water flows past.
pages.pageDescription: Close side view of silver bony fish shows normal gill covers behind eyes as water flows past.
pages.state: No human lung graphic in fish; no universal claim every fish never breathes air.

pages.text: The whale’s calf was born alive and drinks milk made by its mother. Feeding young with milk is a mammal trait.
pages.imageBrief: Adult female blue whale and smaller calf swim closely; calf at mother’s underside in an accurate nonexplicit nursing position. Exact continuity: No bottle, udder hanging like cow, or milk cloud; natural cetacean anatomy.
pages.imageAlt: Adult female blue whale and smaller calf swim closely; calf at mother’s underside in an accurate nonexplicit nursing position.
pages.pageDescription: Adult female blue whale and smaller calf swim closely; calf at mother’s underside in an accurate nonexplicit nursing position.
pages.state: No bottle, udder hanging like cow, or milk cloud; natural cetacean anatomy.

pages.text: Whales also keep their bodies warm from within. A thick layer of fat helps hold that warmth in the cold sea.
pages.imageBrief: Simple blue-whale body cutaway shows a layer of blubber beneath skin, with cold blue water outside. Exact continuity: Anatomical educational cutaway; no fur coat or blanket; only relevant layer visible.
pages.imageAlt: Simple blue-whale body cutaway shows a layer of blubber beneath skin, with cold blue water outside.
pages.pageDescription: Simple blue-whale body cutaway shows a layer of blubber beneath skin, with cold blue water outside.
pages.state: Anatomical educational cutaway; no fur coat or blanket; only relevant layer visible.

pages.text: Some sharks give birth to live young, too. Sharks are fish. That one clue alone cannot tell us “mammal.”
pages.imageBrief: A sandbar shark swims through shallow coastal water with small shark pups nearby, all with visible gill slits and natural fin anatomy. Exact continuity: No birth depicted; sharks remain fish; no whales in this comparison scene.
pages.imageAlt: A sandbar shark swims through shallow coastal water with small shark pups nearby, all with visible gill slits and natural fin anatomy.
pages.pageDescription: A sandbar shark swims through shallow coastal water with small shark pups nearby, all with visible gill slits and natural fin anatomy.
pages.state: No birth depicted; sharks remain fish; no whales in this comparison scene.

pages.text: Scientists use several clues, including body features and how animals are related. Whales belong with mammals despite their fishlike outline.
pages.imageBrief: Return to blue whale and calf, emphasizing lungs at surface and mother-calf relationship without a collage of unrelated animals. Exact continuity: No new symbolic family-tree labels; same whales as earlier.
pages.imageAlt: Return to blue whale and calf, emphasizing lungs at surface and mother-calf relationship without a collage of unrelated animals.
pages.pageDescription: Return to blue whale and calf, emphasizing lungs at surface and mother-calf relationship without a collage of unrelated animals.
pages.state: No new symbolic family-tree labels; same whales as earlier.

pages.text: Dolphins are mammals, too. Like whales, they breathe air and feed their young milk, although they spend their lives in water.
pages.imageBrief: A bottlenose dolphin with a calf swims near surface at natural scale, single blowhole visible on adult. Exact continuity: Dolphin is cetacean; no gills, scales or blue-whale twin blowholes.
pages.imageAlt: A bottlenose dolphin with a calf swims near surface at natural scale, single blowhole visible on adult.
pages.pageDescription: A bottlenose dolphin with a calf swims near surface at natural scale, single blowhole visible on adult.
pages.state: Dolphin is cetacean; no gills, scales or blue-whale twin blowholes.

pages.text: The ocean tells us where these animals live. Their connected features tell us more about the groups they belong to.
pages.imageBrief: Final wide scene shows blue whale and calf, distant dolphin pair and school of fish sharing the ocean without mingled anatomy. Exact continuity: Natural spacing and relative scale; no claim all mammals live in ocean.
pages.imageAlt: Final wide scene shows blue whale and calf, distant dolphin pair and school of fish sharing the ocean without mingled anatomy.
pages.pageDescription: Final wide scene shows blue whale and calf, distant dolphin pair and school of fish sharing the ocean without mingled anatomy.
pages.state: Natural spacing and relative scale; no claim all mammals live in ocean.

oral.prompt: Why are swimming in the ocean and giving birth to live young not enough by themselves to identify a mammal?
oral.listenFor: Many different groups share water, and some fish bear live young; mammal traits include milk and other related features.

visual.prompt: Where does the whale take in air?
visual.lookFor: At the blowholes on top of its head above the surface.

levelRationale: App E weighs multiple classification criteria, rejects two tempting single-clue rules and introduces a concrete exception. Cross-page comparison and qualification carry more conceptual load than simply naming features.

title: Keep the Water in the Garden

storyBibleReview.topicQuestion: How can a garden keep useful moisture around roots without simply adding more water?
storyBibleReview.progression: Observe dry surface versus moisture below, trace where water goes, compare mulch and targeted watering, then apply checking before watering again.
storyBibleReview.synthesis: Checking soil and reducing avoidable loss help use water where plants need it; extra watering is not always the answer.

scienceSources.title: EPA WaterSense: Landscaping Tips
scienceSources.evidence: Mulch reduces evaporation and moderates soil temperature; appropriate irrigation and soil conditions reduce avoidable water use.

scienceSources.title: EPA WaterSense: Outdoors
scienceSources.evidence: Outdoor water conservation includes efficient watering and avoiding waste.

scienceSources.title: Oregon State University Extension: Conserving water in your yard and garden
scienceSources.evidence: Soil moisture checks, mulch and slower targeted irrigation help conserve water; needs depend on soil and plants.

setting: An established vegetable bed in a school garden across three mornings, with an afternoon soil check between the first two. Zoe and Kit inspect with an adult gardener nearby, warm medium skin, short brown hair, plain green shirt and tan trousers.
coverBrief: Zoe gently lifts straw mulch to look at dark moist soil near a vegetable plant while Kit holds a small blue watering can with its spout lowered.

pages.text: The garden soil looks pale and dry on top. Kit lifts the watering can, but Zoe kneels beside a plant first.
pages.imageBrief: Kit holds a blue watering can while Zoe crouches beside an established leafy plant with pale surface soil. Exact continuity: Can not pouring; adult gardener visible nearby; roots not exposed.
pages.imageAlt: Kit holds a blue watering can while Zoe crouches beside an established leafy plant with pale surface soil.
pages.pageDescription: Kit holds a blue watering can while Zoe crouches beside an established leafy plant with pale surface soil.
pages.state: Can not pouring; adult gardener visible nearby; roots not exposed.

pages.text: The gardener helps them check below the surface. The soil underneath is darker and still damp. The top did not tell everything.
pages.imageBrief: Adult gardener uses a blunt trowel to open a small shallow inspection hole away from the plant stem; children see damp soil below. Exact continuity: Avoid damaged roots; adult does digging; dry surface and damp lower soil contrast.
pages.imageAlt: Adult gardener uses a blunt trowel to open a small shallow inspection hole away from the plant stem; children see damp soil below.
pages.pageDescription: Adult gardener uses a blunt trowel to open a small shallow inspection hole away from the plant stem; children see damp soil below.
pages.state: Avoid damaged roots; adult does digging; dry surface and damp lower soil contrast.

pages.text: Plant roots take up water from the soil. Water left on a hot path cannot help these roots in the same way.
pages.imageBrief: Cutaway shows roots within moist bed soil and a separate paved path outside the bed with a small puddle. Exact continuity: No roots magically stretching through pavement; water use relationship concrete.
pages.imageAlt: Cutaway shows roots within moist bed soil and a separate paved path outside the bed with a small puddle.
pages.pageDescription: Cutaway shows roots within moist bed soil and a separate paved path outside the bed with a small puddle.
pages.state: No roots magically stretching through pavement; water use relationship concrete.

pages.text: Some soil water escapes into the air as invisible vapor. This change is evaporation, and sun and wind can speed it up.
pages.imageBrief: Sunny garden scene shows exposed soil and leaves moving in a light breeze; no visible steam rising from ordinary ground. Exact continuity: Water vapor explicitly invisible; no decorative arrows mistaken for vapor.
pages.imageAlt: Sunny garden scene shows exposed soil and leaves moving in a light breeze; no visible steam rising from ordinary ground.
pages.pageDescription: Sunny garden scene shows exposed soil and leaves moving in a light breeze; no visible steam rising from ordinary ground.
pages.state: Water vapor explicitly invisible; no decorative arrows mistaken for vapor.

pages.text: The gardener spreads clean straw over the bare soil. This covering is mulch. It slows water loss and shades the ground.
pages.imageBrief: Adult spreads a thin even layer of clean straw around established vegetable plants while children watch. Exact continuity: Straw away from stems; leaves above mulch; no burial of plants.
pages.imageAlt: Adult spreads a thin even layer of clean straw around established vegetable plants while children watch.
pages.pageDescription: Adult spreads a thin even layer of clean straw around established vegetable plants while children watch.
pages.state: Straw away from stems; leaves above mulch; no burial of plants.

pages.text: Zoe leaves space around each stem. Mulch should cover the soil, not pile up against the plants. They check beneath it later.
pages.imageBrief: Zoe gently shifts straw away from a plant stem, leaving a clear small ring of soil. Exact continuity: Adult nearby; mulch level even; no new watering yet.
pages.imageAlt: Zoe gently shifts straw away from a plant stem, leaving a clear small ring of soil.
pages.pageDescription: Zoe gently shifts straw away from a plant stem, leaving a clear small ring of soil.
pages.state: Adult nearby; mulch level even; no new watering yet.

pages.text: Another morning, the soil near the roots is becoming dry. Kit waters slowly beside the plants, keeping water off the path.
pages.imageBrief: Kit slowly pours from small blue can at soil level beside plants; Zoe watches the dampening root zone. Exact continuity: Explicit later morning; no puddle or runoff; spout stays above soil.
pages.imageAlt: Kit slowly pours from small blue can at soil level beside plants; Zoe watches the dampening root zone.
pages.pageDescription: Kit slowly pours from small blue can at soil level beside plants; Zoe watches the dampening root zone.
pages.state: Explicit later morning; no puddle or runoff; spout stays above soil.

pages.text: A little at a time lets water soak in. If water runs away, pouring faster will not put more around the roots.
pages.imageBrief: Close view shows water soaking into bed soil beneath the can spout with path remaining dry. Exact continuity: Illustrative conditional statement; no demonstrated flooding needed.
pages.imageAlt: Close view shows water soaking into bed soil beneath the can spout with path remaining dry.
pages.pageDescription: Close view shows water soaking into bed soil beneath the can spout with path remaining dry.
pages.state: Illustrative conditional statement; no demonstrated flooding needed.

pages.text: The next morning, they lift the straw and check again. The soil is damp, so the watering can stays by the gate.
pages.imageBrief: Zoe lifts straw to reveal dark damp soil while Kit places the blue can beside the garden gate. Exact continuity: Same bed and plants; no precise universal schedule or invented measurement.
pages.imageAlt: Zoe lifts straw to reveal dark damp soil while Kit places the blue can beside the garden gate.
pages.pageDescription: Zoe lifts straw to reveal dark damp soil while Kit places the blue can beside the garden gate.
pages.state: Same bed and plants; no precise universal schedule or invented measurement.

pages.text: Leaves stand above the covering of straw. The children have saved water by keeping it useful, without leaving the plants thirsty.
pages.imageBrief: Final wide garden view shows healthy leafy vegetables, even straw cover, dry path and blue can resting at gate. Exact continuity: No miraculous overnight growth; adult gardener nearby; conservation supported by observed soil state.
pages.imageAlt: Final wide garden view shows healthy leafy vegetables, even straw cover, dry path and blue can resting at gate.
pages.pageDescription: Final wide garden view shows healthy leafy vegetables, even straw cover, dry path and blue can resting at gate.
pages.state: No miraculous overnight growth; adult gardener nearby; conservation supported by observed soil state.

oral.prompt: Why do the children check under the soil or mulch before watering?
oral.listenFor: Surface color can mislead; soil near roots may already be moist. Checking helps avoid unnecessary watering.

visual.prompt: What do they find beneath the straw, and what do they do next?
visual.lookFor: Damp dark soil; they leave the watering can at the gate.

levelRationale: App E connects observation, hidden soil moisture, evaporation, mulch and conditional watering decisions across several days. The ending depends on checking evidence rather than following a fixed routine.
